NEW YORK (CNN) — Ariel Binns is an adorable, bright, sociable 6-year-old who bears a striking resemblance to Sasha Obama, the younger daughter of the president.

Binns, a young model from Brooklyn, New York, is in first grade, and her likeness to the first daughter has drawn attention in the fashion world. Harper’s Bazaar magazine featured her alongside model Tyra Banks in a photo layout depicting an African-American family living in the White House. In one image, Binns appeared beneath a large wooden desk, evoking a famous scene from the presidency of John F. Kennedy.

In fashion, a strong public image can have enormous commercial power — particularly when that image is tied to a prominent and energetic first family.

“Marketers are finally waking up to it — you know — black is beautiful,” said David Rogers, a global branding specialist. Rogers said he expects African-American models to become more visible in fashion photography because of the Obama family’s influence.

“It’s just going to become part of the fabric of the fashion imagery of pop culture, which is a great thing,” he said.

At Wilhelmina Kids, a New York modeling agency representing children and teenagers, agents report a growing interest in models who resemble the Obama daughters. Marlene Wallach, Wilhelmina’s president, said the demand reflects a broader cultural moment.

“It’s a trend because, what little girl doesn’t want to emulate the first kids?” said Wallach, whose agency represents Binns.

Branding analysts say Sasha and Malia Obama have a different kind of public appeal from Chelsea Clinton or the Bush twins — one that is especially marketable. When the Obama girls wore J.Crew clothing on Inauguration Day, the company’s website received so much traffic that it crashed.

“The most visible, most exciting family in America is this beautiful black family and so people are ready and looking for those kinds of images,” Rogers said. He added that many Americans want to relate to the Obamas and “find some sort of connection with this family.”

But that attention also brings concerns. The Obama family objected when toy company Ty Inc. released African-American dolls called Sweet Sasha and Marvelous Malia, even though the company said the toys were not meant to resemble the Obama daughters. Michelle Obama’s office said it was “inappropriate to use young private citizens for marketing purposes.”

Judy Kuriansky, a clinical psychologist in New York, said well-known families often struggle with that issue.

“I can certainly understand Michelle Obama being protective of her children,” Kuriansky said. “Many celebrities in Hollywood feel that way too. They don’t want their children exposed to the public, because once the child is exposed to the public image, not only are they owned, but they could be used in many different ways and it takes away from the child growing up as a normal, average child.”

Even so, others argue that the visibility of Sasha and Malia can have a beneficial cultural impact by offering a prominent, positive image of young African-American girls.

When asked whether she thinks the Obama daughters could create new opportunities for her own daughter, Ariel Binns’ mother, Dawn Crooks, said, “I think it will. I hope it does.”

Rogers said that, in the larger picture, the use of look-alike models could help push diversity in fashion and media to an entirely new level.

**How Sasha and Malia Obama helped reshape fashion’s idea of visibility — and raised questions about marketing young people**

When Malia and Sasha Obama entered the White House in 2009, they were 10 and 7 years old — children suddenly living at the center of American political symbolism. They were not celebrities by choice, and their parents repeatedly asked the public to respect their privacy. Still, every cardigan, winter coat, party dress and sneaker photographed during those years could become a cultural talking point.

Over time, the Obama sisters’ public image became part of a broader conversation about fashion, advertising and representation — not because they modeled professionally or endorsed brands, but because their visibility challenged long-standing assumptions about who gets to be seen as stylish, aspirational and commercially influential.

### A new kind of fashion influence

The “Obama effect” on fashion was most often associated with Michelle Obama, whose support of both major designers and emerging labels could boost sales and visibility overnight. But Sasha and Malia also played a subtler role.

Their clothing was typically age-appropriate, colorful and accessible — often mixing polished looks for official events with the kind of casualwear familiar to many American families. For fashion watchers, that mattered. The girls were not presented as miniature adults, nor were they styled as distant royal figures. They appeared, as much as possible under extraordinary circumstances, like children growing up.

That relatability gave their appearances an unusual kind of influence. A coat worn at an inauguration, a dress seen during a family trip or a school-appropriate outfit photographed at a public event could prompt online searches and media attention. Retailers and fashion blogs took note, even when the family itself was not promoting anything.

In an industry increasingly driven by visibility, the Obama daughters became examples of how style influence could emerge without traditional advertising.

### Representation beyond the runway

Their presence also carried symbolic weight. For decades, American fashion and advertising were criticized for narrow beauty standards that centered whiteness and excluded many Black girls and women from mainstream images of elegance, innocence, luxury and aspiration.

Sasha and Malia’s visibility complicated that history. As Black girls growing up in one of the most photographed families in the world, they were seen in formalwear, school clothes, vacation outfits and everyday looks. Their image broadened the visual vocabulary of American girlhood in public life.

That representation mattered especially because children’s and teen fashion advertising has often lagged behind adult campaigns in diversity. The Obama sisters’ public presence did not single-handedly transform modeling, but it coincided with rising pressure on brands to feature more models of color, more natural hairstyles and a wider range of identities in youth-oriented campaigns.

Fashion companies, magazines and advertisers increasingly recognized that consumers wanted images that reflected the country more accurately. The visibility of the Obama family — including Sasha and Malia — helped normalize that expectation.

### Advertising without endorsement

The commercial impact, however, came with ethical complications. Sasha and Malia did not choose to be fashion influencers. They were children of a president, not brand ambassadors.

That distinction is important. When a celebrity adult wears a designer outfit, the public often assumes some level of intention, whether through styling, gifting or partnership. With children, especially children in political families, the equation is more sensitive. Brands may benefit from attention generated by a child’s image even when there is no endorsement and no consent to commercial use.

This raises a central concern: Where is the line between reporting on public figures and exploiting children for marketing?

Media coverage of the Obama daughters sometimes drew criticism when it focused too closely on their appearances, behavior or clothing. The Obama White House generally tried to shield them from excessive attention, and news organizations periodically debated whether stories about their style were appropriate at all.

Those concerns have only become more urgent in the social media era, when images of public children can circulate instantly and be repurposed by brands, fan accounts or influencers. A young person’s outfit can become content; content can become traffic; traffic can become profit.

### The problem of “aspirational” children

Fashion and advertising have long used youth as a symbol — of freshness, innocence, trendiness or family values. But marketing children presents risks. It can intensify scrutiny of their bodies, encourage consumer pressure among young audiences and blur the boundary between admiration and commodification.

For Black girls, the stakes can be even more complex. Studies and advocates have long warned that Black children are often “adultified” — perceived as older, less innocent or more responsible than their peers. In fashion coverage, that can mean praising poise and sophistication while forgetting the person being discussed is still a child.

The Obama sisters were often described as graceful and mature, but ethical coverage required remembering that they were minors living under unusual public pressure. Their clothes could be culturally significant without turning them into products.

### A lasting influence

Today, Malia and Sasha Obama are adults, and their public appearances continue to draw attention. But the legacy of their childhood visibility remains tied to a particular moment in American culture: the first Black first family, the rise of digital fashion commentary and a growing demand for more inclusive representation.

Their impact on fashion and advertising was not the result of campaigns or contracts. It came from being seen — and from what their presence made visible. They helped expand mainstream images of Black girlhood, style and aspiration at a time when the fashion industry was being pushed to change.

At the same time, their experience serves as a cautionary tale. Representation matters, but so does consent. Visibility can inspire, but it can also expose children to unwanted commercial and public scrutiny.

The challenge for fashion media, advertisers and audiences is to hold both truths at once: Sasha and Malia Obama’s image helped influence a more diverse cultural landscape, but children should never be treated as marketing tools simply because the public is watching.

**In New York, a Young Model’s Familiar Look Sparks a Bigger Conversation About the Obama Family’s Cultural Legacy**

NEW YORK — On a brisk afternoon in Manhattan, Ariel Binns moved through a small photo studio with the practiced confidence of someone much older. Between flashes of the camera, she laughed with her mother, adjusted the collar of a denim jacket and waited patiently as a stylist smoothed a stray curl.

Ariel, a child model gaining attention in New York’s commercial and fashion circles, has drawn notice not only for her poise but for something more unusual: many people say she bears a striking resemblance to Sasha Obama, the younger daughter of former President Barack Obama and former First Lady Michelle Obama.

For Ariel and her family, the comparison is flattering — but not the whole story.

“She’s Ariel first,” said a family member accompanying her at a recent shoot. “The resemblance may make people look twice, but her personality is what people remember.”

In a city where image, identity and opportunity often intersect, Ariel’s growing visibility reflects a broader fascination with the Obama family — a family whose influence has extended far beyond politics and into fashion, publishing, entertainment, education and popular culture.

### A Familiar Face in a Changing Industry

New York’s modeling world has long been shaped by recognizable looks and cultural moments. Casting directors often seek children who can project warmth, confidence and relatability for campaigns ranging from clothing lines to school-themed advertisements. Ariel’s look — youthful, expressive and polished — has made her a natural fit for family-focused brands.

But the Sasha Obama comparisons add a different layer. Sasha, who spent part of her childhood in the White House, became one of the most recognizable children in America while remaining largely shielded from public life by her parents. As she and her sister Malia grew up, they became symbols of a modern, high-achieving Black American family navigating extraordinary visibility with grace and privacy.

That association can carry commercial power. In advertising, visual references to admired public figures often evoke trust, aspiration and familiarity — even when no formal connection exists.

“A resemblance to someone beloved or widely recognized can create immediate emotional recognition,” said a New York branding consultant. “But the challenge is making sure the individual isn’t reduced to that resemblance.”

For Ariel, that means building a career on her own terms.

### The Obama Effect

More than seven years after leaving the White House, the Obama family continues to occupy a rare space in American culture. Barack Obama remains a major political and literary figure, while Michelle Obama has become a global brand of her own — a bestselling author, speaker, producer and advocate for health, education and women’s empowerment.

Their post-White House ventures have had measurable commercial impact. Books by both Barack and Michelle Obama have sold millions of copies worldwide. Their production company, Higher Ground, has worked with major streaming platforms and helped bring documentaries and scripted projects to broad audiences. Michelle Obama’s fashion choices — from emerging designers to major luxury labels — have often led to increased attention and sales for the brands she wears.

The family’s influence is especially meaningful in Black cultural life. For many Americans, the Obamas represented a new image of Black excellence on the global stage: intellectual, stylish, family-centered and commercially powerful without being defined solely by celebrity.

That visibility has shaped everything from children’s books and dolls to school posters, graduation speeches, fashion editorials and social media aesthetics. The Obama image — polished but approachable, aspirational but grounded — continues to be reproduced and reinterpreted in American consumer culture.

### Representation and Responsibility

Ariel’s emergence in New York modeling also points to a larger shift in the children’s fashion and advertising industries. Brands are under increasing pressure to reflect a wider range of families, skin tones, hair textures and cultural backgrounds. The demand for authentic representation has opened doors for young models of color, particularly Black girls who historically saw fewer images of themselves in mainstream campaigns.

Still, the attention around children in modeling comes with concerns. Parents, agencies and brands must balance opportunity with privacy, education and emotional well-being. Comparisons to famous figures can create excitement, but they can also place expectations on a child who is still developing her own identity.

Those close to Ariel say they are careful to keep the experience age-appropriate. Modeling, they emphasize, is something she enjoys — not a burden.

“She likes the clothes, the cameras, the people,” her family member said. “But when the shoot is over, she’s still a kid.”

### More Than a Look-Alike

In the studio, Ariel seemed less concerned with celebrity comparisons than with the immediate thrill of the day: a rack of outfits, a playlist she liked and the encouragement of adults telling her she was doing a good job.

That may be the most human part of her story. In a culture quick to draw connections to famous names, Ariel’s future will depend not on looking like someone else, but on becoming herself.

The resemblance to Sasha Obama may have sparked curiosity. But in New York — a city built on reinvention — Ariel Binns is learning how to turn a familiar face into an original story.
